info.title: LicenseManager API
info.description:
Public API. Authenticate with an organization API key, or with a token scoped to a customer, license or machine on the endpoints that accept one.

## Conventions

- **Errors** answer `{ "error": { "code", "message" } }`. Branch on `code`, which is stable, not on `message`. Each response lists the codes it can return, except `404`, which answers `not_found` unless it says otherwise. Unexpected errors answer `500` with `internal_error`.
- **Validation** errors answer `422`, not `400`, with the `validation_error` code and an `issues` array giving the `path` and `message` of each invalid value.
- **Unknown body fields are ignored**, not rejected: sending a field an endpoint doesn't accept, like `policyId` to `updateLicense`, changes nothing and doesn't fail.
- **Strings** are trimmed before they're validated and stored. Emails are stored lower cased.
- **Updates** only change the fields that are sent. A field sent as `null` is cleared, when it can be.
- **Dates** can be sent with any offset, and are always returned in UTC, like `2026-01-15T09:30:00.000Z`. Calendar months and days are counted in UTC.
- **Ids** are 8 letters and digits, after `test_` for test products and their resources.
- **Lists** are paginated with `page` and `pageSize`. Items with the same value for the `sort` field are ordered by id, so pages are stable, but items created or deleted between two requests shift the pages. Items without a value for the `sort` field come last in ascending order, and first in descending order, unless the endpoint says otherwise.
- **Test products** are sandboxes of a live product. Test API keys only reach test products, live API keys only live ones: the others answer `404`, as if they didn't exist. Sessions and tokens reach both.

apiKey.name: x-api-key
apiKey.description: Organization API key. `Authorization: Bearer <key>` is also accepted. Live keys (`pk_…`) only reach live products, test keys (`test_pk_…`) only test products: the others answer `404`.

token.description:
Short-lived token scoped to a customer, license or machine, signed with HS256. Its claims:

- `typ`: `customer`, `license` or `machine`, the type of resource the token is scoped to.
- `sub`: id of that resource.
- `scope`: space separated permissions, among `customer:read`, `customer:write`, `license:read`, `license:write`, `license:cancel`, `machine:read` and `machine:write`. A write permission implies the other ones of its resource: `license:write` implies `license:read` and `license:cancel`. Without `scope`, the token can't do anything.
- `exp`: expiration time.

Only the endpoints that say so accept tokens: the others answer `403` with `token_not_allowed`, as do the endpoints that don't accept its type. A token without the endpoint's permission answers `403` with `insufficient_scope`. The token reaches the resource it's scoped to, the ones below it and the ones above it: a license token reaches its customer and machines, but not the customer's other licenses. Resources it doesn't reach answer `404`.

A token can't be revoked: it works until it expires, unless the resource it's scoped to is deleted, which makes it answer `401` with `invalid_token`. Tokens are created by `createCustomerToken`, `createLicenseToken` and `createMachineToken`, with an API key or a session, or with a token for the resources below it: a customer token creates license and machine tokens, a license token machine tokens. Portal links (`createPortalLink`, `requestPortalLink`) hold customer tokens too.

license.description:
JWT signed with the Ed25519 key of the product's organization (`alg: EdDSA`, `kid`: id of the key). Its claims:

- `iss`: name of the organization. It changes when the organization is renamed: check `aud` rather than `iss`.
- `aud`: id of the product. Test and live products share the organization's key, so check `aud` to refuse the tokens of a test product.
- `sub`: license key.
- `fp`: fingerprint of the machine.
- `mv`: the license's `maxVersion.version`, like `"2.3"`, so the application can check the versions it updates to offline. `null` when it allows every version.
- `iat`: when the token was issued.
- `nbf`: two hours before `iat`, so machines whose clock is behind accept the token.
- `exp`: the license's `maxOfflineDurationSeconds` after `iat`, or when the license expires if that's sooner.

fingerprint.description: Identifies the machine. Unique within the license. Compared exactly, case included: a different fingerprint is another machine.

version.description: Version of the application running on the machine, like `"1.4.2"`. maxVersion.description:
Latest version of the product the licenses created with this policy can use. `null` allows every version. Defaults to `null`.

- `fixed`: up to a hard-coded `version`. `"2"` allows every 2.y.z version: its minor versions and bug fixes. `"2.3"` allows every 2.3.z version: its bug fixes.
- `lock`: every version released during some time after the license is created, then only the updates of the version reached by then. The major version locks `majorAfter` the creation of the license, then the license only gets the minor versions and bug fixes of its major version. The minor version optionally locks `minorAfter` it, never sooner than the major version, then the license only gets the bug fixes of its minor version. `{ "type": "lock", "majorAfter": { "value": 1, "unit": "months" }, "minorAfter": { "value": 12, "unit": "months" } }` allows every version released during the month after the license is created, then the minor versions and bug fixes of the major version reached by then until the end of the first year, then only the bug fixes of the minor version reached by then. `majorAfter` at 0 allows minor versions only, and both at 0 allows bug fixes only: no updates.

Bug fixes are never locked: a hard-coded version has no patch number, like `"2.3.1"`, and a lock only locks major and minor versions.

Never shorter than `majorAfter`, whatever the length of the months: 1 month is longer than 28 days but may be shorter than 31. `0` locks it when the license is created. `null` to never lock it.

LockMaxVersion.description: The licenses can use every version released after their creation, until their major version locks `majorAfter` it, then the updates of their major version until their minor version locks `minorAfter` it, if ever. Bug fixes are never locked.

lockMajorAt.description: When the major version of the license locks: it then only gets the minor versions and bug fixes of the major version released by then. Once reached, within the hour, the major version of the latest stable release by then is hard-coded in `version`, unless a version already is, and the lock is cleared. A lock reached before any stable release is cleared without hard-coding anything. `null` when it's never locked.

lockMinorAt.description: When the minor version of the license locks: it then only gets the bug fixes of the minor version released by then, within the hard-coded major version when there's one. Never before `lockMajorAt`; without it, the major version locks along with the minor version. Once reached, within the hour, the major and minor version of the latest stable release by then is hard-coded in `version`, unless a minor version already is, and the lock is cleared. A lock reached before any matching stable release is cleared without hard-coding anything. `null` when it's never locked.

LicenseMaxVersion.description: Latest version of the product the license can use: its hard-coded `version`, else the versions released before its locks. All `null` when it can use every version.

post.description:
Checks the license key of the product on a machine and returns a token the application can verify offline with the organization's public key. Doesn't need authentication.

The license must allow the `version`: up to its `maxVersion.version` when it has one, like `"2.3"` for every 2.3.z version and older. Its `maxVersion.lockMajorAt` and `maxVersion.lockMinorAt` are enforced once they hard-code `maxVersion.version`, within the hour they're reached. When it doesn't, the error's `latestAllowedVersion` is the latest release of the product the license allows, so the application can offer to install it.

The machine with the `fingerprint` is created when the license has none, and activated when it's deactivated, unless the license is already active on its maximum number of machines. A machine that's already active is never refused for the maximum number of machines, even when it was lowered below the number of active machines. Its `version`, and its `name` and `platform` when given, are updated: they can't be cleared.

Unless the product disables `autoMachineChange`, a new machine isn't refused when the license is on its maximum number of machines: it takes the place of the active machine validated the longest ago, which is deactivated with its `overriddenByMachineId` set to the new machine, and recorded as a `machine.deactivated` event. When a machine deactivated this way is validated again, it takes its place back: the machine that overrode it, and the ones that overrode that one in turn, are locked, with their `overriddenByMachineId` set to the machine coming back. A locked machine is always refused, so two machines can't take turns on one place.

The checks run in this order, and the first one failing answers: the license has expired or was canceled, then it doesn't allow the version, then the machine is locked, then it's on its maximum number of machines. Each failure is recorded as a `license.validation_failed` event, except for keys that don't exist.

Changes to the license, like deactivating the machine or shortening its expiration, don't revoke the tokens already returned: the application only sees them when it validates its key again, at the latest when its token expires.

post.description:
Without a `slug`, the product gets one derived from its name: lower cased, without accents and special characters (`Élan Pro 2!` becomes `elan-pro-2`).
When another product of the organization already uses it, a dash and 3 random lowercase letters or digits are appended (`elan-pro-2-k3f`), until the slug is free.

An explicit `slug` is used as is: the request fails with a `409` when it's taken, it's never changed.

Slug uniqueness is enforced by the database, so when concurrent requests end up with the same slug, only one succeeds and the others get a `409`, even without an explicit `slug`. Retrying such a request without a `slug` derives a new one.

The product is created with its default policy, named `Default policy` with the `default` slug, whose settings are given by `defaultPolicy`. Omitted settings default to licenses that never expire, on a single machine, offline for one week, for every version of the product. Unlike `createPolicy`, where `maxMachines` defaults to no limit.

With `isTestFromProductId`, the product is a test product: its id, its slug, and the ids, slugs and license keys of its resources start with `test_` (`TEST-` for license keys), and only test API keys reach it. It starts with copies of the policies, releases, portal settings and `autoMachineChange` of the live product, `defaultPolicy` is ignored. Later changes to the live product aren't copied: reset the test product to copy them again. Test API keys can only create test products, live API keys only live ones.

The license copies the settings of its policy when it's created: later changes to the policy don't affect it. Its key, policy and customer can't be changed afterwards.

patch.description:
The key, policy and customer of a license can't be changed: sending them does nothing.
